title: Load Balancing & Proxies
summary: One server isn't enough. Learn how load balancers spread traffic, how L4 and L7 differ, which algorithm picks the next server, and how proxies fit in.

blocks.markdown:
A **load balancer** sits in front of a pool of servers and distributes incoming requests so no single server is overwhelmed.

- Adds **horizontal scale** — add servers, add capacity.
- Hides individual servers from clients; they talk to one IP.
- Detects unhealthy servers and stops sending traffic to them.
- Two flavours: **L4** (transport layer) and **L7** (application layer).

blocks.subTitle: Traffic flow
blocks.markdown:
Clients reach one address; servers are invisible to them.

Arrow fans out right to three server icons labelled 'Server 1', 'Server 2', 'Server 3'. Label the fan arrows 'distributed requests'. Minimal text, generous whitespace. >>>

- The load balancer's IP is **public**; server IPs are **internal**.
- Return traffic may go directly to the client (DSR) or back through the balancer.

blocks.subTitle: Side by side
blocks.markdown:
The layer determines what the balancer can read.

| | L4 (Transport) | L7 (Application) |
|---|---|---|
| Sees | IP + port + TCP/UDP | HTTP headers, URL, cookies |
| Routes by | IP/port tuples | Path, host, content |
| Speed | Faster, less CPU | Slower, more flexible |
| Example | AWS NLB | AWS ALB, Nginx |

L4 is a **network-level** decision; L7 is an **application-level** decision.

blocks.subTitle: L4 in depth
blocks.markdown:
An **L4 load balancer** operates at the transport layer (TCP/UDP). It sees source IP, destination IP, and port — nothing inside the payload.

- Forwards packets without reading HTTP at all.
- Very fast — almost no overhead per packet.
- Cannot route by URL path or cookie; all it has is the 4-tuple.
- Used when raw throughput matters: game servers, DNS, streaming.

blocks.subTitle: L7 in depth
blocks.markdown:
An **L7 load balancer** operates at the application layer. It terminates the TCP connection, reads the HTTP request, then opens a new connection to the chosen server.

- Can route `/api/*` to one server group and `/static/*` to another.
- Can inspect cookies to implement sticky sessions.
- Enables **SSL termination** — decrypt once at the balancer, forward plain HTTP internally.
- Higher CPU cost than L4 but far more control.

The balancer picks a server using an algorithm.

- **Round robin** — cycle through servers in order. Simple; ignores server load.
- **Least connections** — send to the server with the fewest active connections. Better for long-lived requests.
- **IP hash** — hash the client IP to a server. Same client always hits the same server (natural stickiness).
- **Weighted** — assign a weight per server; a server with weight 3 gets 3× the traffic.

A **health check** is a periodic probe the load balancer sends to each server to confirm it is alive.

- **Active** — balancer sends a TCP ping or HTTP GET; expects a fast 200 OK.
- **Passive** — balancer watches real traffic; too many errors mark a server unhealthy.
- A server that fails N checks is pulled from the pool; it is re-added when checks pass again.
- Without health checks, the balancer happily sends traffic to a crashed server.

blocks.subTitle: Forward vs reverse
blocks.markdown:
A **proxy** sits between two parties and forwards traffic. Direction matters.

| | Forward proxy | Reverse proxy |
|---|---|---|
| Represents | The **client** | The **server** |
| Client knows it? | Yes — configured in browser/OS | No — client thinks it IS the server |
| Common use | Corp filtering, anonymity | Load balancing, SSL termination, caching |

A load balancer is always a **reverse proxy** — it fronts your servers.

**Sticky sessions** (session affinity) route all requests from one client to the same backend server for the lifetime of a session.

- Needed when a server holds **in-memory session state** not shared across the pool.
- L7 balancers implement it via a cookie (e.g. `JSESSIONID`); L4 balancers use IP hash.
- Downside: a crashed server loses all its sticky sessions.
- Better long-term: move session state to a shared store (Redis) and drop stickiness.

Load balancing is the key enabler of **horizontal scaling** — adding identical servers instead of upgrading one big machine.

- With a balancer in front, the app tier is stateless; servers come and go freely.
- Pair with auto-scaling: when CPU is high, spin up a server and register it with the balancer.
- Global load balancers (Anycast, GeoDNS) route clients to the nearest data centre. See [network-reliability-observability](network-reliability-observability).
- CDNs apply the same idea to static content. See [cdn-edge-caching](cdn-edge-caching).

Common mistakes:

- **"Round robin is always fair."** Not with long-lived requests — a slow upload ties up a server while others idle. Use least connections instead.
- **"Sticky sessions mean reliability."** No — they make a server a single point of failure for its sessions.
- **"A load balancer can't be a bottleneck."** It can. A single L7 balancer doing SSL termination for all traffic is itself a chokepoint — run multiple in active-active.
- **"L7 is always better."** It costs more CPU and adds latency; use L4 when you don't need content-awareness.

blocks.subTitle: L4 vs L7
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing?**

**L4** routes based on IP and port at the transport layer — fast, no payload inspection. **L7** reads HTTP headers, URLs, and cookies at the application layer — flexible but higher CPU cost. Use L4 for raw throughput; use L7 when you need path-based routing, SSL termination, or sticky sessions.

blocks.subTitle: Forward vs reverse proxy
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?**

A **forward proxy** sits in front of clients and acts on their behalf — common for corporate filtering or anonymity. A **reverse proxy** sits in front of servers and acts on their behalf — the client doesn't know about the real servers. Load balancers, Nginx, and CDN edge nodes are all reverse proxies.

blocks.subTitle: Balancing algorithms
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you choose least connections over round robin?**

When requests have **variable duration** — file uploads, streaming, long polls. Round robin can pile all slow requests on one server while others sit idle. Least connections continuously sends new requests to whichever server is least busy.

blocks.subTitle: Health checks
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are health checks and why are they essential?**

Health checks are periodic probes (TCP ping or HTTP GET) the balancer sends to each server. A server that fails repeatedly is removed from the pool automatically — no engineer needed. Without them, a crashed server keeps receiving traffic and clients get errors.

blocks.subTitle: Sticky sessions
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are sticky sessions and when are they a problem?**

Sticky sessions (session affinity) pin a client to one server. They're needed when session state lives only in that server's memory. The problem: if that server dies, all its sessions are lost. The fix is to externalise session state (Redis) so any server can serve any client — then stickiness is unnecessary.
